newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ministries get 1998 budget-cap letters.
newsitem.headline: French ministries get 1998 budget-cap letters.

text.p: French ministries received letters from Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Tuesday telling them their spending limits for 1998 as the government searches for ways to cut its deficit and qualify for European monetary union while keeping a promise to create jobs.

French newspapers suggested the budgetary balancing act would be pulled off with the help of a cocktail of savings measures, spending reallocations and one-off payments from state-owned firms. A previously announced corporate tax increase and the rising dollar, if it maintains its gains, would also support the government's efforts.

Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was elected on a platform of stimulating a demand-led economic recovery and attacking France's record 12.6 percent unemployment, but has also to reconcile this with cutting the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in preparation for monetary union.

The government has been keeping tight-lipped on the ministry-by-ministry spending decisions which Jospin wrapped up last Friday before heading off for the second leg of a brief summer break in the west of France.

But a few newspapers have carried stories suggesting it will cut the defence budget by around two billion francs ($320 million) next year, that extra funds for job creation will come from rejigging other job creation subsidies and that the government could tap power utility EdF-GdF as well to help get its finances in shape.

Financial daily L'Agefi said on Tuesday that the government has decided to use about 30 billion francs ($4.8 billion) from state-owned utility Electricite de France-Gaz de France's accounts to help plug the hole in next year's budget.

The one-time payment will come from money EdF-GdF has already provisioned for the construction of a Rhine-Rhone canal, the paper said without naming any sources. Jospin's government had cancelled the canal project for environmental reasons.

The 30 billion francs would single-handedly cut about 0.3 percent of GDP from the central government deficit and make it much easier for France to respect the deficit criterion in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union.

If confirmed, the decision would put to rest speculation among analysts about where the government would find a chunk of money to match a 37.5 billion franc payment from state-owned telephone operator France Telecom.
No one at Jospin's office or the finance ministry was available for comment.

French governments routinely tap state-owned companies such as state bank Caisse des Depots for so-called non-fiscal budgetary receipts but the France Telecom payment, which cut 0.45 percent off the deficit, was seen as exceptionally big. Even so, the press has long been speculating that the government would have to raise the amount it took in 1998.

Financial daily La Tribune reported on Tuesday that the defence budget was likely to be cut again next year as allocations for arms programmes would fall to around 82 to 83 billion francs from 84.9 billion francs in the 1997 budget.
The figure represents the mid-point between the 90 billion francs the defence ministry sought and the 75 billion francs the finance ministry demanded, the paper said, citing anonymous sources.

The paper noted the ministry's 1997 budget had already taken a double blow. The previous centre-right government initiated a 1.8-billion-franc credit freeze, which the new Socialist-led coalition made permanent. It then shaved another two billion under a package announced on July 21 to curb France's public deficit.
Those cuts brought the 1997 defence budget down to 84.9 billion from the original 88.7 billion, the paper said.
The government has also reportedly decided to cut back a subsidy for low wage jobs to save about 10 billion francs, the daily Liberation reported on Saturday.

These savings, which Liberation said would go to new jobs-creation programmes, would help Jospin keep a central campaign promise that a plan to create 150,000 youth jobs in the public sector next year would be paid for by reorganising extensive state job subsidies and not by new spending. The jobs plan, which promises to create a total of 350,000 youth jobs in the public sector over the next few years, is expected to cost the government about 10 billion francs in 1998.

The paper reported that a sliding-scale exoneration from payroll charges applied to jobs that pay up to 1.33 times the minimum wage would be lowered, and also altered so it would not apply if employers are already benefiting from another subsidy.
-- Christopher Noble, Paris Newsroom +331 4221 5452 ($ = 6.277 French Francs)
